readings.title: The headline and the small study
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: Lakeside Science Forum discussed a headline claiming that a new study method doubled learning speed. The original report involved twelve volunteers practising one short task. Participants improved, but there was no comparison group using another method. The tutor asked readers to distinguish the observed result from the wider headline. The investigation might inspire further work, yet it did not show that every learner would progress twice as fast in every subject. Reading the study's limits was not the same as rejecting it. It was a way of deciding what claim the available evidence could reasonably support.
knowledgePoints: 阅读：主旨、细节、推断与语境词义

readings.title: The volunteers who answered first
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: A club surveyed members about moving its meetings online. It sent only an online questionnaire and received many favourable responses. Before changing all meetings, the organiser phoned several members who had not replied. Some lacked a reliable connection; others rarely checked email. Their preferences differed from those of the early respondents. The club kept a mixture of meeting formats and made future surveys available in more than one way. A large share of positive answers could not describe the whole membership if the method of asking made some members less likely to answer.

readings.title: A graph with a missing beginning
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: A newsletter showed a graph in which a small rise in recycling looked dramatic. A reader noticed that the vertical scale began close to the lowest observed value rather than at zero. The figures themselves were accurate, but the visual impression encouraged an exaggerated interpretation. The editor added the complete scale information and a second graph showing the wider range. Readers could then see both the small change and its direction. Good presentation did not require hiding progress. It required giving viewers enough context to judge the size of that progress for themselves.
knowledgePoints: 阅读：主旨、细节、推断与语境词义

readings.title: An explanation worth changing
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: A school gardening club believed that one patch grew poorly because its soil lacked nutrients. Adding compost produced little improvement. A member then noticed that water collected there after rain. The club checked drainage and revised its explanation. Nobody treated the change as proof that the first question had been foolish. Keeping a record of the unsuccessful attempt helped show why the new possibility deserved attention. An investigation progressed because its explanation could change when observations did not fit. Defending the original idea at all costs would have made the records less useful.
knowledgePoints: 阅读：主旨、细节、推断与语境词义

translation.stem:
Translate the following original passage into Chinese. Preserve the meaning and logical relationships.

A convincing story is not always a convincing explanation. Before accepting a claim, readers should ask how the evidence was collected and what else might explain the result. Uncertainty does not make an investigation worthless. Stating it honestly helps others judge what the findings can support.
translation.referenceAnswer: 令人信服的故事并不总是令人信服的解释。在接受一种说法之前，读者应当询问证据是怎样收集的，以及还有什么可能解释这一结果。不确定性并不会使调查失去价值。诚实地说明不确定性，有助于他人判断研究结果能支持哪些结论。
translation.explanation: 参考译文仅示范一种表达。评分时关注信息完整性、转折和条件等逻辑关系；意思准确且中文自然的其他译法同样有效。

criteria.name: 意义完整与准确
criteria.description: 准确传达各句核心信息、对象和逻辑关系；按遗漏或误译程度酌情扣分。

criteria.name: 中文表达
criteria.description: 中文自然通顺，句间衔接合理；不拘泥于英语词序。

criteria.name: 细节与规范
criteria.description: 关键词译法贴合语境，指代清楚，标点和文字规范。

knowledgePoints: 英译汉：语义准确与逻辑衔接

writing.stem:
Write an English response of about 120 words to the following original simulation task. Use your own examples and organise your ideas clearly.

Explain why readers should examine evidence behind a scientific claim. Use an everyday example and offer two useful questions to ask.
writing.sampleAnswer: Readers should examine evidence because an attractive headline can make a limited finding sound universal. Suppose a report says that a new study technique greatly improves learning. Before changing every habit, I would ask who took part and whether the results were compared with another method. A small group practising one task may provide a useful starting point without proving that the technique works for all subjects. I would also ask whether another factor could explain the improvement, such as extra practice time. These questions do not require rejecting unfamiliar ideas. They help us decide how much confidence a claim deserves. Recognising uncertainty allows us to remain curious while avoiding conclusions stronger than the available evidence.
